column3: Directly establishes separate communal accounts: each has what it earned and is not questioned about the other.
Connects criminality with an acquired state and consequence, supporting the focus on owned wrongdoing.
Its loss in the hereafter only broadly supports consequences attaching to those who act.
It repeats 2:134 verbatim, adding no further clarification after the earlier direct parallel.
The preceding ayah sets the same two-sided guidance and error frame that 34:25 answers without mutual accusation.
Mutual questioning supplies only a secondary contrast to the focus ayah's refusal to make the sides answer for one another.
Its warning that people will be questioned reinforces personal accountability, though not the reciprocal separation of accounts.
Its guidance-error contrast extends the prior contextual polarity while leaving liability implicit.
Making the path of criminals distinct supports wrongdoing as an identifiable, acquired course.
Future questioning reinforces accountability, but lacks the focus ayah's allocation of acts to opposing sides.
The next ayah completes the sequence: God gathers the two sides and decides between them in truth.
It distinguishes the accountability of created agents from the one not answerable for His act, adding a different asymmetry.
God's awareness of what people do is relevant but does not clarify the focus ayah's reciprocal disclaimer.
The assurance that acts are not overlooked supports the focus on accountable doing.
Divine knowledge and sight of deeds is a general accountability parallel; its V12 route is contrast evidence.
Its closing notice that deeds are not overlooked repeats the accountability theme already established more directly.
The continuation rejects attributed partners, but adds less to separate liability than the adjacent ayat already do.
Knowledge of deeds at the fixed term gives only a general final-account setting.
It exposes claims of obedience before God who knows deeds, without dividing each side's account.
It shows a follower's harmful orientation and resulting destination, supplying a secondary agency-and-consequence parallel.
Knowledge of concealed and open conduct joins hidden disposition to responsibility rather than allowing evasion.
Rejected excuses and the eventual report of deeds show that assertions cannot transfer or erase one's account.
Provision and its measure do not materially clarify separate responsibility for deeds.
Mutual questioning among a group offers a contrast in which responsibility is contested rather than assigned away.
Its challenge to claims about partners echoes the surrounding polemic but not the focus ayah's account allocation.
The dispute over provision and feeding only remotely parallels the guidance-error frame.
Naming the criminals at their consequence supports the link between committed wrong and its owner.
It makes hatred no excuse for unjust conduct, clarifying that hostile relations do not discharge one's own duty.
The scene of disputation contributes only a broad image of parties contesting blame.
Unfounded testimony is recorded and its speakers questioned, sharply linking a claim to those who made it.
The overwhelming scene of the Hour does not clarify the focus ayah's distribution of liability.
The confession of manifest error is a general consequence parallel without a distinct account relation.
Its reference to criminals adds only the already-covered category of accountable wrongdoers.
Creation, warning, and turning away do not add a route to the focus formulation.
Blaming criminals for misguidance usefully raises outside influence, against which the focus preserves each side's own deeds.
The recurring treatment of criminals supports regular consequence for wrongdoing, though the individual allocation remains unstated.
The recorded book presents each person's acts as present and counted, a concrete basis for non-transferable account.
The wish for a return shows regret but does not clarify responsibility's division.
Its question about prior messengers tests a shared claim about partners, extending the surrounding challenge to attribution.
The designation of a criminal people supplies only a broad collective counterpart to the focus.
Pharaoh's pursuit and its consequence give only a remote agency-and-outcome parallel.
Return to the knower of hidden and visible brings deeds into disclosure, reinforcing final answerability.
The statement that criminals are not questioned in that setting is a procedural contrast, not the focus's mutual disclaimer.
Pharaoh's leading his people astray distinguishes an influencing agent, while the focus guards against collapsing all accounts together.
Truth prevailing despite criminals' dislike does not add a specific account relation.
The suspension of questioning on that Day is only a contextual contrast to accountable questioning.
Guidance benefiting oneself supplies a useful self-directed responsibility parallel.
The separation of criminals makes the consequence of their own course visibly distinct.
Steadfastness and divine sight of deeds offer only general ethical accountability.
The destruction of wrongdoers after clear messages links a community's acts to its consequence.
A further mutual-questioning scene is redundant after 37:27 and adds little to the focus.
Its relation of persons and their acts adds a distinct theological frame for accountable doing.
Successors are observed in how they act, reinforcing responsibility across changing communities.
The passage through criminals' hearts concerns reception of a message, not the allocation of deeds between sides.
It explicitly joins no wrong to recompense for what people used to do, grounding just personal return.
Provision for creatures does not clarify liability for actions.
It repeats the mutual-questioning image already covered without bringing it close to the focus's formula.
The reciprocal declaration of my deed and your deed is the closest direct parallel to separate responsibility.
Following the way rather than desire offers only an indirect guidance contrast.
Universal questioning confirms comprehensive accountability, though not the two-sided separation in the focus.
False attribution of provision is paired with questioning, showing claims remain with their makers.
Following desire and losing guidance is a remote orientation parallel.
It states that good and bad action returns to the self before return to the Lord, directly supporting owned consequence.
The denial of help gives a general consequence setting but no account allocation.
Guidance after being astray does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
The removal of lineage and mutual questioning at the trumpet powerfully isolates persons from inherited social claims.
The prediction of regret has no substantial connection to separate liability.
The message reaching the heart does not clarify the focus's reciprocal accounting.
Questioning in the gardens is a distant contrast to the focus ayah's disavowal of questioning the other side.
The announcement of a learned son is unrelated to the focus.
Guidance and misguidance lead to distinct outcomes, but the account allocation is not developed.
Calling a people criminal supplies only the general category already well represented.
The inability of any patron to avail another adds a useful non-transferability boundary.
Its account of a message entering criminals' hearts remains remote from reciprocal liability.
The immediate dialogue explicitly contests whether leaders diverted followers, sharpening the focus's refusal to answer for the other's acts.
Despite the guidance-misguidance frame, people are questioned about what they did, preserving accountable action.
It explicitly assigns an alleged fabrication to its speaker and separates it from the others' criminality.
Hereafter loss is a further generic consequence of wrongdoing, now largely redundant.
God's awareness of deeds occurs in a different instruction and adds little beyond earlier accountability cards.
The sound heart motif does not clarify the focus's relation between opposing accounts.
Refusing to support criminals gives a secondary agency boundary but not separate accounting.
The messenger's lack of control over harm or guidance only broadly fits the surrounding dialogue.
Kinship will not benefit and God separates people by deeds, denying family-based transfer of standing.
The following reply names sustained social pressure yet ends in recompense for what they did, preserving both influence and own acts.
All affairs return to God, who is not unaware of deeds, reinforcing the final-account horizon.
The flood narrative and command do not clarify the focus ayah's liability relation.
Its distinction between submitters and criminals is a broad moral sorting already covered more concretely.
Concealed conduct remains witnessed against its doers, making ignorance no escape from one's acts.
Hostility can drive a community into a repeated destructive pattern, adding causal warning without removing its responsibility.
The fragment recalls inquiry about deeds but adds no independent content after fuller questioning cards.
The oath by what is unseen does not clarify responsibility or separate accounts.
Excuses spoken outwardly are tested against what is in hearts and against deeds known to God.
Oppression is upon the selves that commit it before return and report, directly supporting self-borne consequence.
The rescue of Lot and his household does not illuminate the focus's two-sided accounting.
Its ritual and marital regulations do not offer a material inter-ayah route to the focus.
Inheritance allocations do not clarify the focus ayah's responsibility for deeds.
The isolated report of speech adds no usable clarification.
The marking threat has no material link to the focus's account relation.
A false utterance is attributed to those who say it, but the legal context is otherwise remote.
Reliance on protectors besides God echoes the surrounding partner polemic but adds no separate-liability clarification.
The reciprocal formula that each side has its own deeds is a direct parallel to the focus ayah's separated accounts.
What each self earns for and against itself provides a compact principle of personally borne consequence.
Whoever commits a sin earns it only against the self, directly excluding displacement of culpability.
No soul earns except against itself and no bearer carries another's burden gives the clearest general rule behind the focus.
Guidance and error return to the self, followed by the explicit rule that no bearer carries another's burden.
The reciprocal declaration of our deeds and your deeds closely restates the focus ayah's non-entanglement of accounts.
The proposal that others bear a group's sins exposes the very attempted transfer of responsibility refused by the focus.
The denial that they can carry others' sins, alongside liability for their own misleading, distinguishes influence from transferred guilt.
No burdened self carries another's burden supplies an explicit boundary for the focus ayah's separate liability.
The repeated rule that no bearer carries another's burden confirms that accountability cannot be shifted across persons.
For us our deeds and for you your deeds is a near-verbatim reciprocal counterpart, joined to the end of disputation.
The stated principle that no bearer bears another's burden directly clarifies why neither side answers for the other's acts.
A person having only what it strives for makes earned consequence personal and non-transferable.
Every self being held for what it earned reinforces the focus ayah's ownership of action and account.
No self can avail another at all on that Day gives an eschatological boundary to reliance on another's standing.
Seeing even an atom's weight of good makes individual acts and their return explicit.
Seeing even an atom's weight of evil complements the focus ayah's concern with personally owned wrongdoing.
